subject: English
passage:
The following text is adapted from Sinclair Lewis's 1920 novel Main Street. Gopher Prairie is a fictional town in Minnesota.

[Gopher Prairie] consisted of broad avenues all remarkably similar to one another, and narrow side streets even more remarkably similar to one another, occupied by families equally similar to one another, who all rose and retired at the same times, with the same conversations over the same meals, to pursue the same aspirations, and for whom every season was the duplicate of the last and the next, and every generation the echo of those before and after.
prompt: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To emphasize the conformity of both the town's layout and the lives of its inhabitants
choices.B: To explain the restricted social mobility available to the town's families
choices.C: To suggest how the routine nature of the town causes residents to feel disconnected from history
choices.D: To demonstrate that the consistency of life in the town creates a strong sense of community

explanation:
Choice A is the best answer. The author describes Gopher Prairie as having avenues and streets that are all very similar and families who live similarly and pursue the same aspirations. This repetition of similarities emphasizes how everything in Gopher Prairie conforms to the same pattern.

Why B is incorrect:

Choice B is incorrect. While the text mentions that all the families "pursue the same aspirations," it never explains what those aspirations are or suggests they're limited by social barriers. Besides, the idea that they all share aspirations is just one of several similarities among the townspeople described in the text.
